stem: Which statement best distinguishes a fit-tested N95 filtering facepiece respirator from a surgical mask in a healthcare respiratory-protection context?

options.A: A surgical mask forms a tighter face seal than an N95 and is preferred for inhalation protection from airborne particles.
options.B: A fit-tested N95 is a tight-fitting respirator that filters airborne particles; a surgical mask is loose-fitting and does not provide the same reliable aerosol respiratory protection.
options.C: An N95 and a surgical mask provide equivalent fit and wearer protection from aerosolized particles when both are worn correctly.
options.D: An N95 is intended mainly for splash protection and does not filter small airborne particles.

rationale: Current CDC/NIOSH healthcare respiratory-protection guidance states that NIOSH Approved filtering facepiece respirators such as N95s are tight-fitting devices that filter at least 95% of airborne particles and require fit testing within a respiratory-protection program. Surgical masks are loose-fitting medical devices that can provide barrier protection against splashes and large droplets but do not provide a reliable level of wearer protection from aerosolized particles because they do not form the same facial seal. Therefore B is correct. A, C, and D misstate the fit or particulate-protection properties of the devices.
educational_objective: Differentiate N95 respirators from surgical masks by recognizing the N95's tight facial seal, fit-testing requirement, and particulate respiratory protection.

source_original.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a fit-tested N95 filtering facepiece respirator from a surgical mask in a healthcare respiratory-protection context?

options.B: A fit-tested N95 is a tight-fitting respirator designed to filter airborne particles; a surgical mask does not provide the same fitted respiratory protection.

source_original.rationale: NIOSH-approved N95 filtering facepiece respirators are designed to filter airborne particles and must fit the wearer's face adequately as part of a respiratory-protection program. Surgical masks are loose-fitting source-control/barrier devices and do not provide the same fitted respiratory protection.

correction_summary: Retained the N95-versus-surgical-mask construct and key B. Tightened B to current NIOSH language, added the ≥95% particulate-filtration context in the rationale, and removed TB-specific wording from the distractor so the item tests device properties rather than a disease cue.

audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item accurately distinguishes fit/seal and aerosol particulate protection without claiming surgical masks have no barrier function at all.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because surgical masks are loose-fitting and do not provide tighter respiratory protection than N95s.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because fit and reliable aerosol protection are not equivalent between the two device types.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because N95s are specifically designed to filter airborne particles.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B correctly describes both the N95 and surgical-mask characteristics without overclaiming either device's role.
audit_findings.cueing: All options compare the same two device types on fit/protection characteristics.
